source: Fu, Wang, Tian, Zhao (2025) Deep Think with Confidence (DeepConf)
finding: Stops sampling more traces when the vote among independent answers already agrees (consensus stop, tau=0.95), and also kills low-confidence traces mid-generation using the model's own token log-probs (not verbalised confidence). Tokens counted end to end.
numbers: Models DeepSeek-8B, Qwen3-32B, GPT-OSS-120B; AIME24/25, BRUMO25, HMMT25 plus GPQA-Diamond; 64 reruns each. Budget K=512. DeepConf-low cuts 43-79% of tokens vs majority vote, DeepConf-high 18-59%. DeepSeek-8B AIME24 86.7 -> 92.5 (low) at -77.9% tokens; GPT-OSS-120B HMMT25 92.8 -> 92.0 (-76.2%). Consensus stop alone (Qwen3-32B AIME24): -15.4% tokens at K=32 and -52.8% at K=512 with no accuracy change (low); -22.0% and -54.7% (high). tau=0.90/0.85 gives up to 69.6% savings but -0.26 pp accuracy in the low variant. GPQA-D accuracy moves by -0.4 to +0.3 pp with -21% to -52% tokens (appendix).
quote: model-internal confidence signals to dynamically filter out low-quality reasoning traces
limits: Mostly math; one non-math set (GPQA-D, multiple choice). No code or agent task. Confidence is from log-probs, so it needs open-weight or logprob access. Authors name overconfident wrong answers as the main failure (GPT-OSS-120B HMMT25 drop). Not compared head to head with DEER or verbalised self-confidence.
agent_relevance: Agreement among independent attempts is a cheap stop rule that cost no accuracy at tau=0.95. Candidate for the G6 stop when no real check exists. Gap 1 only partly closed: no equal-token duel against self-confidence stopping, almost no non-math data.

source: Aggarwal, Madaan, Yang, Mausam (2023) Let's Sample Step by Step: Adaptive-Consistency
finding: Stops sampling when a Beta-posterior says the leading answer will stay in front. At equal average sample cost it beats plain self-consistency in accuracy. For code it clusters executed outputs.
numbers: 17 datasets, 3 models (GPT-3.5-turbo, Vicuna-13B, Code-davinci-002). Sample cuts: 3.3x math (-0.1% acc), 2.9x commonsense (-0.2%), 3.8x symbolic (no change), 2.4x code (+0.4% acc); up to 7.9x; by model 4.4x GPT-3.5, 1.9x Vicuna, 3.4x Code-davinci. Max 40 samples for reasoning, 50-100 for code. GSM8K at average cost 10 samples: about +3% accuracy over self-consistency at the same cost. The Beta criterion is about four orders of magnitude faster than Dirichlet/CRP versions with similar accuracy.
limits: Single seed for the main table (paper says so). Cost counted in samples, not tokens. 2023 models. Code agreement is on executed outputs, which is a real execution check.
agent_relevance: Agreement-based stopping beats a fixed sample count at equal average cost, including on code. Supports a cheap stopping module in the scaffold. No self-confidence rival tested.

source: Li, Yuan, Feng, Pan, Wang, Sun, Wang, Li (2024) Escape Sky-high Cost: Early-Stopping Self-Consistency (ESC)
finding: Samples in small windows and stops when a whole window gives one answer. The ESC vote matches full self-consistency in over 99% of cases.
numbers: Average sample cut: MATH -33.8%, GSM8K -80.1%, StrategyQA -76.8%, CommonsenseQA -78.5%, Coin Flip -84.2%, Last Letters -67.4%. Intersection with full SC 99.13-99.96% (GPT-4, GPT-3.5, Llama-2-7b). MBPP code, GPT-3.5-Turbo, window 5, max 30 samples: SC 62.18 vs ESC 62.15 using 6.79 samples (-23.21). Window 8 for MATH, 5 elsewhere; 10 runs averaged.
limits: Smaller saving on code (-23% samples) and on MATH (-34%) than on easy tasks. Window size is a hand-set knob. Samples counted, not tokens.
agent_relevance: Second independent agreement-stop method. Savings shrink where agreement is rare (hard maths, code). Gap 1: shows agreement stopping transfers to MBPP at no accuracy cost.

source: OPPO AI Agent Team (2025) Scaling Test-time Compute for LLM Agents
finding: First systematic test of parallel (best-of-N, beam, DVTS), sequential (reflection) and verifier methods on a web agent. Plain best-of-N beat tree-like searches. Reflecting at every step did not help; reflecting only when the step score is very low helped a little.
numbers: GAIA validation, 165 tasks, GPT-4.1 base. Baseline 55.76; best-of-N about +8 points (overall about 63); BoN-wise best on Level 3; beam search and DVTS about equal to baseline. Reflection every step 55.15 (L1 71.7, L2 51.16, L3 34.62 vs baseline 66.04, 58.14, 26.92). Reflection thresholds: <8 gives 53.33, <5 gives 52.12, <2 gives 56.36. BoN width 1, 2, 4 rose with width. Mixed-model pass@4 74.55.
limits: Single runs, no confidence intervals, 165 tasks (one task = 0.6 points). Table text extraction was garbled; BoN overall value read as about 63. Tree search failed because the verifier signal was poor.
agent_relevance: On an agent task a plain repeat-and-select beats clever search, and always-on reflection can hurt. Supports 'reflect only when a signal says so' (G6/G12). Gap 2: shows non-monotone cells by level but no quality-vs-token curve.

source: Li et al. (2025) S*: Test Time Scaling for Code Generation
finding: Hybrid of parallel samples plus up to R rounds of debugging with real test execution, then pairwise selection with generated distinguishing inputs. Model-written tests alone did not beat public tests.
numbers: LiveCodeBench v2, 12 models. Pass@1 gains from +8.6 (o1-mini) to +25.0 (Qwen-Coder-7B); GPT-4o-mini + S* beats o1-preview by 3.7; R1-Distill-32B reaches 85.7 vs o1-high 88.5. Parallel N: Qwen2.5-Coder-7B gains over 35 points at N=64; QwQ-32B-Preview rises from 50% (N=1) to 80% (N=32) but plateaus beyond N=32. Two debug rounds lift QwQ-32B-Preview from 72.6 to 74.2. Generated-test selection gave no gain over public-tests-only; adaptive input synthesis did.
limits: Ablations on LiveCodeBench with N=8, single settings, no confidence intervals. Authors' own baselines.
agent_relevance: On code, a real execution check (public tests) is the reliable anytime signal; model-written tests add noise. Supports G3/G6 keep-best-by-check. Shows a parallel-coverage plateau (N>32) for a reasoning model.

source: Jain et al. (2025) R2E-Gym: Procedural Environments and Hybrid Verifiers for Scaling Open-Weights SWE Agents
finding: On SWE-bench Verified, selecting among many agent runs plateaus for each single verifier type, and a hybrid of execution-based and execution-free verifiers breaks the plateau. It also compares where to spend extra rollouts: test-writing agent vs code-editing agent.
numbers: R2E-Gym-32B: Pass@1 34.4%; Pass@26 (1 run at T=0 plus 25 at T=0.8/0.9) 64.4%. Execution-based and execution-free verifiers plateau at 43.7% and 42.8% Best@K; hybrid reaches Best@26 = 51.0%. Compute split: editing rollouts 16 -> 21 moves Best@K from 47.6% to 48.4% (+0.8); 5 extra test-agent rollouts give 49.3% (+1.7). Regression tests alone 42.9 -> 47.4; adding generated reproduction tests helps further. Removing trajectory-level information drops Best@26 from 42.8 to 37.6.
limits: One model, one benchmark (500 items); single run per configuration, no intervals. Cost not measured in tokens. Verifier is trained.
agent_relevance: Gap 5: first empirical stage-split result: moving budget from the solver stage to the check stage gave about twice the marginal gain. Gap 2: selection quality plateaus (about 43%) then jumps when a different signal is added, so a one-signal stop rule would stop in the wrong place.

source: Hassid, Synnaeve, Adi, Schwartz (2025) Don't Overthink it: Preferring Shorter Thinking Chains for Improved LLM Reasoning
finding: Within one question, shorter sampled reasoning chains are more often right than the longest. short-m@k runs k chains in parallel, halts after the first m finish and votes among them. Compared at equal thinking tokens against majority@k.
numbers: Models LN-Super-49B, R1-32B, QwQ-32B, R1-670B; AIME24, AIME25, HMMT, GPQA-D; 20 generations per question, k from 1 to 10. Shorter chain up to 34.5% more accurate than the longest for the same question. short-1@k uses up to 40% fewer thinking tokens at similar accuracy (LN-Super-49B: 57% accuracy at about 60% of majority@k compute); short-3@k beats majority@k at all budgets with up to 33% wall-time cut. At larger k majority@k overtakes short-1@k in 3 of 4 models. QwQ-32B short-1@k declines slightly with k.
limits: Reasoning models on math and GPQA only. Subsets resampled from 20 generations (no fresh independent runs). Depends on wrong answers having longer chains.
agent_relevance: Parallel attempts with early halting on the first finishers is a strong equal-token baseline and argues against extending one long trace. One side of gap 3; the sequential side is weaker for untuned models (d14).

source: Lin et al. (2026, ICLR) Plan and Budget: Effective and Efficient Test-Time Scaling on LLM Reasoning
finding: Splits a query into sub-questions, then allocates a token budget per sub-question with a decay schedule (front-loaded), uniform split, or one global cap. Direct test of how to split a fixed budget across stages.
numbers: MATH-500, NaturalInstructions, TravelPlanner (agentic planning); DS-Qwen-32B, QwQ-32B, DS-Llama-70B, o4-mini. Claims up to +70% accuracy, -39% tokens, +193.8% E3 (accuracy squared per token). Local vs global budget E3: MATH-500 DS-Llama-70B 5.16 -> 5.89 (+14.1%); NaturalInstructions QwQ 1.61 -> 2.00 (+24.2%); TravelPlanner QwQ 0.39 -> 0.52 (+33.3%). Uniform local split already beats a global cap; decay schedules add little (DS-Qwen-32B MATH-500 E3: uniform 5.64, polynomial 5.92, best decay about 6.07). On NaturalInstructions uniform is competitive. Table 7 MATH-500 with run SDs: Plan-and-Budget 90.04+-0.46 at 1336 tokens vs vanilla 89.76+-0.26 at 2105.
limits: E3 is the authors' own metric. Differences between schedulers are small, a few percent, few seeds. The planning step costs tokens (modest latency overhead). Sub-question difficulty is estimated by an LLM, not measured.
agent_relevance: Gap 5: the only direct study found. Per-stage budgets beat one global cap; the exact schedule matters little; front-loading helps on maths and planning. Our scaffold can start with fixed shares front-loaded on the early states. No greedy marginal-gain or learned-profile comparison exists.

source: Wu, Miroyan, Chan, Darrell, Norouzi, Gonzalez (2026, ICML) Are Large Reasoning Models Interruptible?
finding: Cuts the reasoning at different points and forces an answer. Quality rises with how late the cut falls (anytime behaviour), but cut traces show reasoning leakage (reasoning moved into the answer), panic under speed-up requests, and self-doubt with updated information.
numbers: Qwen3-8B, GPT-OSS-20B (high effort), Magistral-Small-1.2 in the main text; GPT-OSS-120B, DeepSeek-R1, Nemotron-3-Nano in appendix. GSM8K, MATH-500, AIME24/25, LiveCodeBench v6. 16 trials for AIME, bootstrapped 95% CIs. Earlier hard interrupts give lower accuracy in most cases; exceptions: Magistral on AIME and coding where late interrupts slightly beat no interrupt. Leakage gives answers up to 10x longer after early hard interrupts. Up to 60% performance drop when updates arrive late. Over 90% of new errors under speed-up come from panic; about 80% of update-driven errors from self-doubt. A prompt guidance postfix mitigates self-doubt.
limits: Open-weight reasoning models only; closed APIs cannot be interrupted mid-reasoning (GPT-5.4-Mini tested by proxy). Math plus one code set.
agent_relevance: Gap 7: shows what cutting a trace does on non-trained models: accuracy roughly monotone in cut time, but the answer segment is not safe unless reserved or checked, and tokens spent in the answer hide extra compute. Supports reserving a final-answer segment and counting answer tokens in budgets (G12).

source: Lanham et al. (2023) Measuring Faithfulness in Chain-of-Thought Reasoning
finding: Early-answering test: truncate the written chain after each sentence and ask for the answer. On many tasks the answer is already fixed from the first sentences, so extra reasoning changes little; this varies strongly by task.
numbers: Early-answering area-over-curve (higher means the answer changes more as the chain grows) ranges from 0.02 to 0.44 across the multiple-choice tasks, with LogiQA 0.44 and ARC (easy) at 0.12 or lower; adding-mistakes AOC from 0.07 to 0.52. Chains truncated at every sentence; 175B-class Anthropic model.
limits: Single 2023 model; multiple-choice answers (guess floor); some table cells could not be mapped to task names in the extracted text. Measures post-hoc reasoning, not anytime quality directly.
agent_relevance: Gap 7: non-trained model, cut chain, forced answer: curves are flat for easy tasks and rising for hard ones. A per-task curve is needed; a single global cut rule is unsafe.

source: Hochlehnert, Bhatnagar, Udandarao, Albanie, Prabhu, Bethge (2025, COLM) A Sober Look at Progress in Language Model Reasoning: Pitfalls and Paths to Reproducibility
finding: Re-evaluates recent small-model reasoning methods with many seeds. Seed noise on 30-item benchmarks is as large as the reported gains. Most RL gains vanish; SFT gains hold.
numbers: Pass@1 standard deviation 5 to 15 points across 20 seeds for nine models on AIME24, AMC23, MATH500; one question shifts AIME24 by 3.3 points and AMC23 by 2.5. About K>=30 seeds needed for stable AIME24 means. Reported-vs-measured gaps up to 17.0% in some re-evaluations. Authors use 10 seeds for AIME24/AMC23, 3 for MATH500 and paired tests (p<0.01 and p<0.001). L1 models did not beat the R1-Distill baseline; OpenRS claimed 10-15% gains but no significant gain on replication; only DeepScaleR and FastCuRL were significant; s1.1-7B is among the SFT models.
limits: Does not test AnytimeReasoner or s1 budget forcing directly. 1.5B-7B models, math only.
agent_relevance: Gap 10: confirms that single-run gains on 30-item sets (s1 Wait +6.7, AnytimeReasoner +3.9 on AIME24) are inside seed noise, so our tests need many seeds and paired tests. No direct replication of those two papers was found.

source: Balachandran et al. (2025) Inference-Time Scaling for Complex Tasks: Where We Stand and What Lies Ahead
finding: Nine models, eight tasks, repeated independent calls (parallel) or repeated calls with critic feedback (sequential). Which is better depends on the task and on the quality of feedback.
numbers: On AIME 2025, parallel best-of-n beats sequential for GPT-4o (parallel up to 256 calls, sequential up to 32); GPT-4o accuracy grows about linearly in log calls. On TSP-easy (100 instances) sequential is more efficient; GPT-4o rises from 42% to 95% with superscaling. TSP-hard shows no gain. For o1, sequential with a hybrid verifier beat parallel with a perfect verifier. More tokens do not mean more accuracy; token use per instance varies widely (cost nondeterminism).
limits: Best-of-n with a perfect verifier is an upper bound, not a deployable result. Sequential success depends on critic quality (the model itself here).
agent_relevance: Gap 3: gives a task-level reason for the disagreement: sequential wins when feedback is informative (TSP), parallel when it is not (AIME). The crossover depends on critic quality more than on token count.

source: Qu, Yang, Setlur, Tunstall, Beeching, Salakhutdinov, Kumar (2025) Optimizing Test-Time Compute via Meta Reinforcement Fine-Tuning (MRT)
finding: Treats the reasoning stream as episodes and measures cumulative regret over the token budget (area under the quality-vs-budget curve). Shows standard outcome-reward models do not make steady progress per episode, and that trimming the thought block and forcing an answer works for R1-type models.
numbers: MRT: 2-3x relative gain over GRPO's gain, about 1.5x token efficiency vs GRPO and 5x vs the base model (1.5B, AIME24/25, AMC23 etc.); Llama-3.1 backtracking setting 1.6-1.7x. In problems needing 41-45 episodes the accuracy of later episodes does not rise and sometimes falls, while majority over earlier-episode answers does better. Extrapolates to 2x larger budgets than trained.
limits: Trained method (RL fine-tuning), not training-free; math; 1.5B-8B models. The authors note R1 ends its thought block after a time-limit statement.
agent_relevance: Gap 2 and 4: gives the right measure for anytime quality (regret over the whole budget curve, not one point) and shows late-episode degradation. Gap 7: premature trimming plus forced answer is workable on R1-type models.

source: Zeng, Cheng, Yin, Zhou, Qiu (2025) Revisiting the Test-Time Scaling of o1-like Models: Do they Truly Possess Test-Time Scaling Capabilities?
finding: For QwQ, R1-Distill and LIMO, correct solutions are shorter than incorrect ones on the same question. Longer chains carry more self-revision ('Wait'), and revision turns correct answers into wrong ones more often than the reverse. Parallel scaling gives better coverage and scalability than sequential revision.
numbers: MATH-500, AIME (90 AIMO validation questions), Omni-MATH, GPQA-Diamond (198). Forced continuation with 'Wait' or 'Alternatively' for 40 extra steps lengthened solutions almost linearly. Sequential revision: correct-to-wrong exceeded wrong-to-correct for several models. Parallel: 10 samples gave larger coverage gains than 10 sequential revisions on AIME. Shortest Majority Vote beats plain majority.
limits: Models not trained for budget forcing; s1 fine-tuned on 1k traces with Wait extension, which may explain its different result. Math and GPQA only.
agent_relevance: Gap 3: a testable reason for the Ghosal vs s1 split: whether the model was trained to use continuation. For untrained models, extending one trace with Wait is net harmful and parallel wins. Do not use Wait extension on untuned models without a check.

source: Zhang et al. (2025) Reasoning Models Know When They're Right: Probing Hidden States for Self-Verification
finding: A probe on hidden states predicts whether an intermediate answer is correct, and its score is calibrated. Used as a stop rule it cuts tokens at equal accuracy and beats a fixed-chunk stop.
numbers: R1-Distill models 1.5B-32B; GSM8K, MATH, AIME, KnowLogic. In-distribution ROC-AUC above 0.7 and ECE below 0.1; over 0.9 ROC-AUC for the 32B model on AIME. Early exit on MATH with R1-Distill-Llama-8B (10K cap): Thr 0.85 gives 88.2% accuracy (same as no exit) with about 24% fewer tokens; Thr 0.9 gives 88.6% (same) with 19% fewer. At similar tokens, probe exit 87.4% (Thr 0.8) vs static exit about 82.5%, up to +5%. Probes do not transfer stably across domains (GSM8K/MATH to AIME poorly calibrated; logic to math fails).
limits: Needs hidden-state access and a probe trained per dataset. Early exit tested on MATH only.
agent_relevance: Gap 1: a trained internal signal also beats a fixed-count stop at equal tokens, but not tested against agreement. Not available for black-box models.

source: Fu, Chen, Zhu et al. (2025) Efficiently Scaling LLM Reasoning with Certaindex (Dynasor)
finding: Certaindex is a stability measure: how much intermediate answers (or agreement among samples, or reward scores) stop changing. Forced mid-reasoning answer probes show when the right answer first appears. Used to stop early or to give less to stable queries.
numbers: Probe-in-the-middle on AMC23: median 2.7K tokens produced, correct answer typically available by a median of 830 tokens. Certaindex vs steps-to-solution correlation 0.17 to 0.75, mean 0.52 over four settings. Token savings 9-52% across SC, MCTS, Rebase workloads without accuracy loss vs uniform allocation (over 47% for SC on GSM8K, over 50% for Rebase on Math); includes SC on LiveCodeBench. A length-only baseline hurt accuracy. Appendix: curve-fit and per-step thresholds save a further 1-3.4% over a static threshold (SC/MATH 1.18M -> 1.03-1.01M tokens vs 1.05M).
limits: Authors' own system; accuracy parity at their thresholds. A different group (Plan and Budget Table 7, MATH-500) found the Certaindex early-exit baseline lost accuracy (DS-Qwen-32B 81.44% vs 89.76% vanilla). Thresholds need per-workload tuning.
agent_relevance: Gaps 1 and 6: stability of the answer across samples is a cheap difficulty probe and stop signal across algorithms, including code SC. Gap 8: fine-grained prediction beat a static threshold only by a small margin. Others' reproduction conflicts; treat as promising, not settled.

source: Zhang, Zhou, Wang, Wang, Li (2024) Scaling LLM Inference with Optimized Sample Compute Allocation (OSCA)
finding: Learns, from a training set, how to split a fixed sample budget over inference configurations (model, temperature, etc.) with hill climbing. A data-driven split that needs per-problem-category statistics.
numbers: Claims better accuracy than the best single configuration with 128x less compute on code generation (LiveCodeBench) and 25x less on four reasoning tasks; on SWE-Bench better than the default with 3x less compute. Results vary with the fraction of training data used (for example 25% training).
limits: Allocation is over configurations learned offline, not adaptive per item; needs held-out items. Numbers are pass@C with an oracle check. Only abstract, intro and parts of the results were read.
agent_relevance: Gaps 5 and 6: a learned allocation profile exists and works with an oracle check, but it needs a labelled calibration set. It is not a cheap per-item difficulty probe.

source: Li et al. (2026) SelfBudgeter: Adaptive Token Allocation for Efficient LLM Reasoning
finding: Trains the model to write its own token budget before reasoning (budget-guided GRPO), so the user can see the cost and decide to stop.
numbers: Average response length compressed by 61% on math reasoning while keeping accuracy; on MATH500 +3.54 points with response length reduced to 44%. Evaluated on GSM8K, MATH500, AIME2025.
limits: Needs RL training; math only; the budget is self-predicted with no external difficulty ground truth. Only the abstract, intro and result summary were read closely.
agent_relevance: Gap 6: a model can learn to predict its needed length, but only after training; prompted budgets in untrained models are unreliable (s1 control results). No training-free probe matching Snell's 4x saving was found.

source: Heitz (2014) The speed-accuracy tradeoff: history, physiology, methodology, and behavior
finding: Review of the human speed-accuracy tradeoff (SAT). Accuracy is modelled as an exponential approach to an asymptote with an intercept and a rate; separates macro-SAT (between conditions) from micro-SAT (within conditions). Read through a page-reading tool (first 100,000 of 228,000 characters).
numbers: No human-subject figures extracted. A simulation in the review gives deadlines of 225, 325 and 425 ms and accuracies of 50%, 70% and 90% (10,000 observations per condition): a model illustration, not data. SAT experiments need several times more observations than non-SAT designs.
quote: humans can learn to become optimal with sufficient practice
limits: Read via a summarising fetch tool, so exact numbers are limited. Expertise is not discussed in the part read. Whether macro and micro SAT share a source is unresolved. The exponential form is called atheoretical.
agent_relevance: Gap 9: human accuracy vs time is a saturating curve, matching the concave-profile assumption of anytime theory for simple choices only; not evidence for complex expert decisions.

source: Chabris and Hearst (2003) Visualization, pattern recognition, and forward search: effects of playing speed and sight of the position on grandmaster chess errors
finding: Computer-scored blunders of 23 grandmasters under three conditions: classical, rapid (with sight), rapid blindfold. Faster play raised the blunder rate by about a third; removing sight of the board added a little more.
numbers: 1,188 games, 23 grandmasters; 719 true blunders (176 classical, 266 rapid, 277 blindfold). Blunders per 1,000 moves: classical 5.02, rapid 6.85 (+36.5%), blindfold 7.63. Rapid play averaged under one minute per move; classical about 40 moves in 2 hours.
limits: Experts only; no novice comparison; blunder rate, not a move-quality curve. Natural tournament games (Monaco), not a controlled time manipulation.
agent_relevance: Gap 9: for experts a large time cut raises errors only modestly (+36.5%), consistent with recognition doing most of the work early (anytime curve with high early quality). Aspiration-adjustment satisficing was not tested.
